candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Forking-path libertarianism requires indeterminism, but physicalist accounts can supply it through quantum effects and top-down causation.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Brain-level criteria can constrain quantum indeterminacy so that decisions remain reason-responsive without becoming either determined or random.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted elaboration continues Hawkins's answer and explicitly presents a supporting account he has read and plans to discuss further.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It addresses the randomness objection to libertarian choice by describing a mechanism combining alternative possibilities with rational constraint.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's concern that indeterminism may not preserve the libertarian ability to choose among genuinely branching possibilities.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Top-down causation rejects microreductionism because macro-level patterns help determine micro-events and informational patterns evade ordinary closure assumptions.

candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies the anti-reductionist causal architecture needed for the preceding physicalist defense of nonrandom libertarian agency.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's characterization of the physicalist proposal as a rejection of exhaustive micro-level reductionism.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Indeterminism can reappear at the psychological level even when intermediate physical levels are deterministic, making decision-level freedom conceptually coherent.

candidates.loadBearingReason: It independently supports the coherence of decision-level indeterminism and weakens the inference from lower-level determination to determined agency.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Libertarian freedom needs sourcehood and alternative possibilities, but alternative possibilities do not require an objectively branching future.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins explicitly turns from the cited physicalist theory to his own libertarian position and develops it continuously through the possible-world conclusion.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This states Hawkins's central libertarian alternative to both causal determinism and the standard forking-path model challenged by Folley.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's request to distinguish Hawkins's own view from a branching-tracks form of physicalist libertarianism.

candidates.proposition: Hawkins's modal claim may not conflict with the consequence argument because changing the decision by changing the past concedes that a fixed past fixes the decision.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins's claim that one could have chosen otherwise in a possible world whose past and initial conditions were also different.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: The consequence argument wrongly transfers logical dependence from past to present into dependence of agency, control, and sourcehood.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins begins with an explicit diagnosis of the disagreement and sustains the distinction between modal relations and agential causation through the end of his answer.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's objection that Van Inwagen can accept different choices under different pasts while still denying alternatives when the actual past is fixed.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Hawkins and Van Inwagen use 'could have done otherwise' at different modal scopes, and both usages can coexist without contradiction.

candidates.proposition: Causal determinism trivially excludes branching futures, but libertarian freedom can persist under non-causal determinism by combining modal alternatives with agential sourcehood.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Causation is fundamentally an agency-based concept of influence and reasons, so importing mechanistic necessity into it creates a false threat to free will.

candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the idealist foundation for preferring non-causal determination: rational structure explains events without turning agents into externally forced puppets.
